Since Privilege and the Wage Gap are topics that occupy a lot of liberal areas. I figured I would make a case on why the premise is useful, and how it is used flat out wrongly.

Wage Gap studies are always done by Sociology departments. The basic premise behind them is from a tool that is privilege. Neither premise is accurate or useful in comparing individuals, nor are they indicative of anything beyond expected performances based on tells in a community being examined.

Construct: The Construct is a logical structure that is used to represent something. This term has become a buzzword, and is usually misapplied. A construct is just a shorthand. Phrase such as "Gender is a construct" is technically accurate, but doesn't actually mean anything. It merely represents the concept of "Gender" as viewed by a community being examined. That is all. It does not mean anything is true or false. The method is akin to scalar variables, or objects in object oriented programming. A construct has a presumed meaning to the audience.

Privilege: The Sociological meaning of Privilege is a construct. A community is broken into demographics and whatever metrics that are being examined are averaged. The demographic averages are then compared. The ways in which one performs better than another has the term 'privilege'. They should have chosen another term due to the baggage. As is, this is one that is prone to abuse. It cannot be used in reference to individuals. It is just a smoke test for a broad overview of a community. If one demographic performs 'better' in an area, it just indicates that there is something worth examining. But, like a smoke test-smoke doesn't always have fire. The wage gap studies use a privilege construct. They should not be viewed as indicative of anything beyond that smoke test.

When reading them, the reader should also note what exactly is being compared in the privilege construct. Simple comparing men and women via income, or, does it factor age, tenure, career, and education? Does that study simple look at 20-30 year old men broken down by religion for income?

Privilege studies are not meant to be consumed as a regular study. They are just tools like a compass. Simply because there is discrepancy does not mean something shadey is going on. It simply means more factors are required.

An analogy:

If I dig up fifty rocks from my back yard and weigh them, I would find that some weigh more than others. If I leave my 'study' at that, we can infer all sorts of things ranging from a problem regarding where the rocks came from to any other anomaly one can think of. However, discrepancy is all it will show-they are clearly not equal even though they came from the same area.

After density, size, volume: the discrepancies become obvious. The same is true with the wage gap.

The premises are being misused and mishandled. Bad science should be fought against regardless of if anyone is perceived as being harmed by it. Science must stand on it's own merits, or it is religious in nature.
[Science] A note on Privilege Constructs, and the Wage Gap.

Some more general principles I slowly grasped after driving for a while, and some specifics:

  • Safety is about always keeping a margin for error. This means that you'll be doing things that 99% of the time don't give any visible benefit. Don't slowly eat into this margin, saying that "nothing has happened yet"; safety is insurance, where you pay a small amount regularly and hope to never have to need it. Safety requires foresight, unlike many other things which you can wait for reality to give you feedback before adjusting.

  • Predictability helps others avoid hitting you. Many aspects of driving are about being predictable: following traffic laws and lane markings, signaling before turning, not making sudden changes in what you're doing.

  • Don't rush; you're already getting there over ten times as fast as on foot, a few times faster than bus or bicycle. A couple of minutes don't matter.

  • You can take the road rage route, and be angry at others a lot. You can also take the zen driving approach, where you expect other drivers to be careless, and learn to spot them from a distance and give them extra room to do their thing, without putting yourself in harm's way.

  • Keep 2-3 seconds distance behind the car you're following, more in adverse conditions. This gives you plenty of time to respond and stop/swerve if the car stops or crashes in front of you. You have ultimate control of this distance, not the car in front; you can always increase the distance by using your brake.

  • Car damage is at the very least a big headache and probably costly. Even a minor scrape can do a lot. Since you don't normally hit things, you don't have an intuitive sense of how massive a car is and how much force it carries even at low speeds. Take a little extra time to avoid it. In parking lots, park with spaces between other cars, even if it means walking an extra 100 feet to the store.

  • If you realize you're in the wrong lane, go with it rather than suddenly changing lanes unsafely. Go through the intersection and turn around if necessary to get back on course.

  • If you're stopped by an officer, put your hands visible on the wheel. If you want to get something, ask the officer and tell them where you're going to reach; don't just reach suddenly, as they deal regularly with people who are reaching for guns.

  • And for fuck's sake, don't use your phone while driving. This cuts into your safety margin. Reality won't give you feedback about this until you smash into another car or person. That's too late.

If you devote your attention entirely to driving, it can be fun and something you continually improve.

I have ADHD - officially diagnosed and all that. My son has it too. My parents both have it. I guess it's a hereditary thing. My daughter probably has it, but she's disabled in other ways, so we'll likely never see a real manifestation.

My parents first noticed some odd behaviors in me way back when I was three or so. I was having some pretty big thoughts for a three-year-old as well. They talked to a number of docs about it, all of who said I was definitely different and some of them suggested medicating me (ritalin). My father was absolutely opposed to any medication, which is odd because he regularly medicated himself with alcohol - lots and lots and lots of alcohol. That's how he dealt with his issues. 36 ounces of gin every night, seven night a week, for many years. No, I am not exaggerating. Mom was almost as bad. Usually 1/3 to 1/2 a bottle of vodka a night. I grew up in an interesting household.

Anyway, without medication, I was left entirely to my own devices. It helped a little that my folks put me in possibly the best (most advanced) private school in the US. I walked out of eighth grade with some fairly advanced college level education. The downside was all the competition and advanced social stuff - I was a wreck for most of my grammar school years. I socialized more easily with adults than my own peers. And with not knowing I was different (nobody ever said anything), I was often the butt of classroom jokes. To say it was tough is a tremendous understatement. I had to build my own mental structures and practices to help keep my mind focused. Gods it was hard. I was smart enough that when a new concept came up, it took very little for me to entirely understand it. But memorization was always my downfall. Because I didn't want to memorize anything I wasn't going to actively use, I hated it.

High school was a little easier. Teachers there saw I was a little different and I got some leeway.

College was tough at first (I enrolled in a very difficult aerospace engineering school), but then when I got bored with it, I looked for something easier. Changed colleges and wound up with an English degree. Why does this matter? I'll tell you.

I didn't know I was different. Didn't even dawn on me until I was in my late 20s. Then, after things crashed down around me in graduate school, I got a diagnosis. They said it wasn't surprising I never liked school.

Now, I'm a programmer / data-BI jockey, and I've been self-taught in the computer arena for 36 years. Never ever went to school for programming (though I know half a dozen languages and even taught a few classes), never went to school for data or BI, but I'm highly skilled and have an excellent 10 year track record.

The point of all of this is two-fold. First, no matter what anyone says, you can succeed even with a bad case of ADHD. Second, I watched a few people I grew up with get medicated and it turned their minds to jelly.

I manage through brute force and steering myself toward things I enjoy. Sure a few things fall through the cracks now and then, but it really comes down to routine and algorithms for every single thing I do. Every action I make is scripted in advance. Every task I undertake, even for things as simple as leaving the house (I touch every pocket to make sure I have everything) or getting out of the car (I check every switch to make sure everything is off properly) - it's all routine. It sounds a little insane, but after so many years it's just second nature.

Now I suppose you might ask how I keep my mind from wandering. Well, sometimes it's hard. And that's when the brute force kicks in. If I can make my mind actually focus on something hard enough, I can realize a level of intelligence for what I'm focusing on that very few people can understand.

In my weak moments, I've come to know what relaxes me in healthy ways. I love lifting very heavy weights. That's a big mental relaxer for me, and I try to keep regular at it. Sugar is a huge relaxer for me, as is caffeine (makes me focus like a laser and it feels so good), but those have to be indulged in limited quantities for obvious reasons. Sex and orgasms is awesome, but that's in extremely limited supply these days. If you're old enough I'd suggest you find someone with a matching sex drive and have at it. Shooting sports (archery / guns) is great for focusing and relaxing at the same time. I've heard martial arts is an excellent focusing agent, though I've not indulged that.

I sit at the computer a lot attempting to slake my constant thirst for intellectual entertainment. But the internet is a lot like candy. Occasionally I find something interesting what takes some time to digest.

I do drink. But it's weird. I'm Russian / Irish and I'm pretty big so I can drink like a fish (which sucks). I can go and get blasted drunk (that takes a lot) and then not drink for months and not care. Luckily I didn't get the alcoholic thing. But I caution most people with ADHD - stay the fuck away from alcohol. It can destroy you so easily. Just stay away from drugs period. People with ADHD have a thirst for pleasure and satisfaction most regular people can't comprehend. We get very revved up in making ourselves feel good because we feel so disconnected most of the time. Anything to come down and focus - anything to be normal.

So exercise. Eat well. Exercise more. Get plenty of regular sleep. Sleep (or the lack thereof) will kill you. It's so easy to stay up WAY past your bedtime, right? Ya, don't do that. Get in a regular practice of sleeping well and for plenty of time. Healthy sex, and lots of it. And "healthy" can be anything you want (don't limit yourself) - just don't hurt anybody. Know you're different. Actively knowing this really helps. It means both understand your pitfalls and where you underachieve as well as understand where you excel. Because you do excel, don't you? I'll tell you a secret:

ADHD isn't a diagnosis nor is it a disability. Nope. ADHD is a product of evolution. See, as our human minds evolve, we get used to taking in information in greater quantities and of greater complexity. So after a while our brains are used to processing at a higher rate than what's normally offered in life. This is why we get bored so easily. We thirst for input. People without ADHD see this as a disability because it pulls us away from their world - the "normal" world. Well, fuck the "normal" world. Go seek your desired level of input, but understand you're different from most, and try to be productive about it.

Again: routine, exercise, good sex, good food, plenty of sleep. That should get you up and running easily. And don't every let anyone tell you ADHD is a disability. People who say that have small, limited minds who can't stretch beyond their own limits. Ignore them.
